cards.statement: A leading underscore gives an Ansible variable private visibility.
cards.explanation: Ansible applies normal variable scope to names beginning with an underscore; the prefix adds no privacy.
cards.misconception: Underscore-prefixed variables receive private visibility.

cards.statement: `ansible-playbook site.yml -e @release.yml` loads extra vars from the YAML file `release.yml`.
cards.explanation: Prefix a variable file's name with `@` when supplying its contents through `-e`.

cards.statement: Ansible chooses the extra-vars value when the same variable exists in other variable sources.
cards.explanation: Extra vars occupy the top of Ansible's variable precedence order, so competing definitions yield to them.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: Ansible uses an inventory value over a matching variable defined in a role's defaults.
cards.explanation: Role defaults provide starting values at the lowest variable precedence; inventory values override them.

cards.statement: Ansible uses play `vars` value `release: old` after `ansible.builtin.set_fact` sets `release: new`.
cards.explanation: A regular `ansible.builtin.set_fact` host variable outranks play `vars`, so later tasks read `new`.
cards.misconception: Play variables keep priority over variables set during execution.

cards.statement: With play-level `remote_user: deploy`, adding `-u ops` makes Ansible connect as `ops`.
cards.explanation: The play's `remote_user` keyword overrides the command-line `-u` setting, so Ansible connects as `deploy`.
cards.misconception: Command-line connection options override playbook keywords.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: A host's registered variable remains available in subsequent plays of the same playbook run.
cards.explanation: Ansible keeps registered task results as host variables in memory for the current playbook run.

cards.statement: Ansible leaves the registered name undefined when a task's `when` evaluates to false.
cards.explanation: A task skipped by `when` still creates its registered variable containing the skipped result.
cards.misconception: A conditional skip prevents creation of a registered variable.

cards.statement: With `cacheable: true`, `ansible.builtin.set_fact` creates a host variable and a lower-priority fact copy.
cards.explanation: The two copies coexist in the current run; the fact copy is eligible for persistence through a configured fact cache.

cards.statement: Ansible combines keys from repeated dictionary variable definitions as it resolves precedence.
cards.explanation: The default `replace` behavior selects the winning dictionary as a whole, replacing earlier definitions.
cards.misconception: Ansible automatically merges dictionary keys across variable sources.

cards.statement: With `remote_user: deploy` and `ansible_user: ops`, Ansible connects as `ops`.
cards.explanation: The connection variable `ansible_user` overrides the equivalent playbook keyword `remote_user`.

source.title: Controlling how Ansible behaves: precedence rules

cards.statement: Ansible merges values from discovered `ansible.cfg` files while searching for its configuration.
cards.explanation: Ansible uses the first configuration file found in its search order and ignores the remaining files.
cards.misconception: Ansible combines settings from multiple configuration files.

cards.statement: Ansible automatically runs `ansible.builtin.setup` at the start of a play to gather facts.
cards.explanation: The initial gathering step collects managed-host information for use by the play's tasks.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: A play's `gather_facts: false` makes explicit `ansible.builtin.setup` tasks report skipped.
cards.explanation: An explicit `ansible.builtin.setup` task still gathers facts in a play with `gather_facts: false`.
cards.misconception: Disabling play-level fact gathering also disables explicit setup tasks.

cards.statement: With gathering set to `smart`, Ansible reuses a host's facts in later plays of the same run.
cards.explanation: After discovering a host's facts, smart gathering avoids gathering them again as subsequent plays address that host.

cards.statement: Ansible keeps the `ansible_` prefix on system fact keys inside `ansible_facts`.
cards.explanation: Read the OS family as `ansible_facts['os_family']`; system fact keys drop the `ansible_` prefix inside this dictionary.
cards.misconception: Fact dictionary keys retain the prefix shown in setup module output.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.20, Ansible deprecates reading injected top-level fact variables.
cards.explanation: Accessing injected fact variables emits a deprecation warning; read facts through the `ansible_facts` dictionary.
cards.volatilityNote: The default for fact injection is scheduled to change in ansible-core 2.24.

cards.statement: Ansible limits fact collection to matching names when `ansible.builtin.setup` uses `filter`.
cards.explanation: The `filter` option limits returned facts; `gather_subset` controls which groups of facts the module collects.
cards.misconception: The setup filter limits collection rather than the returned data.

cards.statement: Ansible exposes a facts.d file's custom data through `ansible_facts['local']`.
cards.explanation: The local namespace keeps custom facts from `.fact` files separate from built-in system facts.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible refreshes `inventory_hostname` to match `ansible_facts['hostname']` during fact gathering.
cards.explanation: The `inventory_hostname` value comes from inventory, so gathering facts leaves that identifier intact.
cards.misconception: Fact gathering updates the inventory identifier to the system hostname.

cards.statement: After adding a `.fact` file, Ansible needs another `ansible.builtin.setup` call to use it in the same play.
cards.explanation: Re-run `ansible.builtin.setup` after installing the custom fact so later tasks in that play can read it.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible's default memory fact cache supplies gathered facts to the next playbook run.
cards.explanation: The memory cache retains facts for the current Ansible execution; its contents end with that run.
cards.misconception: The default fact cache persists data across playbook executions.

cards.statement: Ansible automatically gathers another host's `ansible_facts` when a task reads them through `hostvars`.
cards.explanation: Access another host's facts through `hostvars` after those facts have been gathered or loaded from a fact cache.
cards.misconception: Looking up a host's facts causes Ansible to collect them on demand.

source.title: Discovering variables: facts and magic variables

cards.statement: Ansible removes failed hosts from `ansible_play_hosts` as they leave the active play.
cards.explanation: The `ansible_play_hosts` list tracks hosts still active in the play and excludes failed or unreachable hosts.

cards.statement: Ansible renders task templates on the control node before sending the task to a managed host.
cards.explanation: The controller resolves template expressions locally and sends the values needed for the task to its target.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.copy` can render Jinja2 expressions inside a source file before transferring that file.
cards.explanation: Use ansible.builtin.template when file contents need Jinja2 rendering. The copy module transfers the source file's existing content.
cards.misconception: The copy module evaluates Jinja2 expressions embedded in source files.

cards.statement: Ansible requires quotes around an inline YAML value starting with a Jinja2 expression such as `{{ name }}`.
cards.explanation: YAML treats an opening `{` as mapping syntax. Quote the entire value so Ansible receives the intended template string.

cards.statement: Ansible substitutes an empty string when a task template reads an undefined variable.
cards.explanation: An undefined variable used in a task's template raises an error rather than becoming an empty string.
cards.misconception: Ansible silently fills missing template variables with empty strings.

cards.statement: Using `default(omit)` lets Ansible omit a module option whose input variable is undefined.
cards.explanation: When an expression resolves to omit, Ansible removes that option from the arguments passed to the module.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, `ansible.builtin.bool` reports a hard error for unrecognized input.
cards.explanation: Unrecognized input produces a deprecation warning while the bool filter still returns a boolean value.
cards.misconception: Unrecognized bool-filter input immediately fails conversion.
cards.volatilityNote: Unrecognized-input coercion is deprecated; the warning is planned to become an error in ansible-core 2.23.

cards.statement: With `recursive=true`, `ansible.builtin.combine` merges the keys of matching nested dictionaries.
cards.explanation: Recursive merging preserves untouched nested keys while applying the supplied overrides inside those dictionaries.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.dict2items` produces two-element lists containing dictionary keys and values.
cards.explanation: The dict2items filter returns a list of dictionaries with `key` and `value` fields, pairing each source key with its value.
cards.misconception: The dict2items filter returns key-value pairs as lists rather than dictionaries.

cards.statement: `ansible.builtin.selectattr` turns matching objects into their selected attribute values.
cards.explanation: The selectattr filter tests the chosen attribute and returns the matching original objects.
cards.misconception: The selectattr filter projects attribute values instead of selecting whole objects.

cards.statement: Ansible's `query()` function returns lookup results as a list, ready for a task's loop.
cards.explanation: The query function is shorthand for `lookup(..., wantlist=True)`, which supplies list results.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, Ansible preserves a list's type when templating a variable as `{{ packages }}`.
cards.explanation: Ansible evaluates variable templates in Jinja2's native mode, preserving a returned list's type rather than converting it to text.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, Ansible returns `{{ range(0, 3) }}` as a list when templating a variable.
cards.explanation: The range function produces a range object. Convert it with `| list` before returning it from an Ansible template.
cards.misconception: Ansible automatically converts a range object into a list at template finalization.

cards.statement: Ansible reads `when: flag` as a raw Jinja2 expression using the variable `flag`.
cards.explanation: A when expression refers to variable names directly. Ansible evaluates the expression as the task's execution condition.

cards.statement: Since ansible-core 2.19, Ansible accepts an arbitrary string result from `when` by default.
cards.explanation: A when condition must return a boolean by default. A string result produces an error instead of implicit truthy evaluation.
cards.misconception: Ansible treats nonempty string results as true conditions.

cards.statement: Ansible combines conditions listed under `when` with a logical `and`.
cards.explanation: Ansible runs the task when each listed condition succeeds; separate list entries narrow the task's execution.

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates `result is failed` from the result's status, even when `result.stderr` is empty.
cards.explanation: The failed test checks the task result's failed status. Empty stderr does not make a failed result successful.

source.title: ansible.builtin.failed test – did the task fail

cards.statement: Ansible evaluates a looped task's `when` condition once before it starts processing the items.
cards.explanation: Ansible evaluates when separately for each loop item, so one task can run for some items and skip others.
cards.misconception: Ansible uses one condition result for the complete loop.

cards.statement: Ansible skips a task looping over `targets | default([])` when `targets` is undefined.
cards.explanation: default([]) supplies an empty list for an undefined variable, leaving no items for the task to process.

cards.statement: The loops guide marks `with_<lookup>` forms as deprecated in favor of `loop`.
cards.explanation: with_<lookup> forms remain supported. The loops guide explicitly says these forms are not deprecated.
cards.misconception: The loop keyword deprecates with_<lookup> syntax.

cards.statement: A `loop` over a nested list flattens one level just as `with_items` does.
cards.explanation: with_items flattens one level implicitly. A loop needs flatten(1) to reproduce that behavior.
cards.misconception: The loop keyword implicitly flattens nested items.

cards.statement: `loop_control.label` changes the value that Ansible passes to the looped task as `item`.
cards.explanation: loop_control.label changes the displayed label; the task still receives the original item.
cards.misconception: The loop label replaces item data.

cards.statement: Ansible reevaluates an `until` condition after rerunning the task, up to its retry limit.
cards.explanation: Ansible evaluates `until` using each attempt's fresh task result. A true result ends retries.

cards.statement: Ansible sets a looped task's overall `changed` result from the final loop item.
cards.explanation: The loop's overall changed result becomes true when any item reports a change, even if the final item reports ok.
cards.misconception: The final loop item's status becomes the complete task's changed status.

cards.statement: Ansible reports a looped task as `skipped` only when every item is skipped.
cards.explanation: The loop's overall skipped status means the complete set of iterations was skipped, rather than just some items.
